opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the way to think about it is that a huge fraction of what we actually do day to day in AI research isn't the "eureka" moment. It's engineering. You have an idea, and then you spend days or weeks implementing it, debugging it, getting the infrastructure to work, babysitting runs, and reading loss curves to figure out whether it's working or whether you've got a bug. The ratio of thinking to doing is surprisingly low, even for really senior researchers.

So the first and most obvious place models help is compressing that loop. If a model can take a well-specified experiment and implement it, run it, and come back with clean results, then a researcher's taste becomes the bottleneck, not their hands. Instead of running three experiments a week, you can run thirty. Research is really an empirical search process, so more shots on goal, with fast feedback, matters a lot.

The second piece is that these tasks are unusually well suited to models. Code is verifiable. Experiments produce numbers. You can tell whether a kernel is faster or whether a change improved the eval. That's exactly the kind of environment where you can train models with reinforcement learning and have them get reliably good, which you can't always do with fuzzier tasks.

Then there's the more speculative part: models contributing research taste themselves. Can they look at a set of results and propose the right next experiment? Can they notice that something weird in a plot is actually important rather than noise? I think that comes later. It's harder to verify, and good taste is built from a lot of accumulated context. But you don't need it for a big speedup. Even if models just act as extremely capable research engineers, you could imagine a single researcher directing what used to be a whole team's worth of experiments.

The caveat is compute. If everyone suddenly has ten times more experimental throughput, you hit the wall of how many GPUs you have. So the acceleration is real, but it'll partly show up as a shift toward smarter use of compute: smaller-scale experiments that predict large-scale behavior, better prioritization, and fewer wasted runs. That's where I think the near-term gains are, and it's already starting to happen.

r001.rationale: The response discusses engineering work and experimental search, but does not distinguish algorithmic discovery from synthetic data driving model capability gains.

r002.rationale: It notes that GPU availability can limit experimental throughput, but does not identify additional compute as a necessary condition for meaningful acceleration.

r003.rationale: It describes models acting as research engineers, but does not say they are easier to bring up to speed on a task than human collaborators.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it already is, in a way that people underestimate. The thing I'd push back on is the framing where "AI accelerating AI research" means some single system sitting there having novel conceptual insights about transformers. That's the sci-fi version. The real version is much more mundane and much more powerful.

Most of what we do day to day as researchers isn't having brilliant ideas. It's engineering. It's writing the data loader, debugging why your loss spiked at step forty thousand, figuring out that two kernels are fighting over memory, setting up the ablation sweep, reading the logs. The idea generation is maybe five percent of the job and the other ninety-five percent is this grind of making the experiment actually happen. And that ninety-five percent is exactly the stuff that models are getting good at.

So the first-order effect is just that each researcher gets to run more experiments per unit time. If I have ten hypotheses and I used to be able to test two of them a week, and now I can test eight, the rate at which the field learns goes up a lot. Research is bottlenecked on iteration speed, and iteration speed is bottlenecked on engineering throughput.

The second thing, which I think is more interesting, is that models change what counts as a feasible experiment. There are a lot of ideas that nobody tries because the cost of trying them is too high relative to the expected payoff. Weird architectures, odd data mixtures, things that require you to rewrite a bunch of infrastructure. When the marginal cost of trying something falls, the space of things you actually explore widens. And some of the really important stuff is going to be in that long tail.

Then there's the taste question, which is what everyone wants to talk about. Can the model actually have good research intuitions? I think that's the hard part and I don't want to pretend we're there. But I also don't think it's magic. A lot of research taste is pattern matching over a huge number of prior experiments, knowing which directions tend to work and which don't, and knowing what the failure modes look like. That's a learnable thing. The models have read every paper. The question is whether they can connect that to the empirical feedback loop, and that's really a question of giving them enough agency and compute to actually close the loop themselves.

The thing I'd watch for is the point where you can hand a model a research direction, not a task, and it comes back a day later with a well-designed set of experiments and a sensible interpretation of the results. We're not quite there. But the distance between "writes most of my code" and "runs most of my experiments" is a lot shorter than the distance we've already covered.

And the reason this matters for timelines is that it's reflexive. If the bottleneck on better models is researcher throughput, and models increase researcher throughput, you get a compounding effect. I don't think it's a hard takeoff, I think there are a lot of other bottlenecks, compute being the big one. But the slope changes. That's the part I think people should be taking more seriously.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI improving research engineering and experimentation, but it does not distinguish algorithmic discovery from synthetic data driving model capability gains.

r002.rationale: It identifies compute as a major bottleneck and says models need enough agency and compute to close the research feedback loop.

r003.rationale: It does not compare how quickly AI research assistants and human collaborators can get up to speed on a task.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is shortening the loop between having an idea and finding out whether it works. A lot of AI research involves implementing something, checking that the experiment actually tests what you intended, waiting for it to run, and then figuring out what the results mean. An AI that can take on substantial parts of that loop could be enormously useful without being better than the best researcher at coming up with ideas.

For example, you could say, “I think this model is failing because of this feature of the training data. Can you design a small experiment that distinguishes that explanation from these two alternatives?” If it can implement the experiment, debug it, and bring back a result you can trust, you’ve made the researcher much more productive.

The harder step is choosing what to investigate. Running ten times as many experiments isn’t necessarily valuable if they’re all answering unimportant questions. You want systems that can notice something surprising, form a useful hypothesis, and update their approach when the evidence contradicts it.

And there are still constraints. You haven’t magically created more compute, and some experiments take a long time. But better judgment about which experiments to run—and getting more information out of each one—could accelerate progress substantially even with the same compute budget.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI helping design and run experiments, but does not distinguish algorithmic discovery from synthetic data driving capability gains.

r002.rationale: It says progress could accelerate “even with the same compute budget,” rather than identifying additional compute as necessary.

r003.rationale: It gives an example of assigning a task to an AI, but does not say AI assistants are easier to bring up to speed than human collaborators.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is how much of the research loop you can hand over. There’s a version where AI helps you write the code for an experiment, which is useful, but you’re still deciding what to try, checking the results, and figuring out what they mean. You haven’t removed the bottleneck if the researcher is still doing all of that.

The more consequential version is a system that can take a question, design experiments, run them, notice when something’s broken, and come back with a result you can trust. Then you can have many more ideas being tested in parallel. A researcher might spend their time choosing promising directions and interrogating the evidence rather than implementing every experiment.

And I wouldn’t assume the first big gains require some extraordinary new insight. A lot of research involves getting the details right: finding bugs, understanding why a run failed, making comparisons fair. If you can do that reliably and cheaply, you can accelerate progress quite a bit.

The hard part is judging whether you’ve actually learned something. Producing plausible explanations is much easier than producing good experimental evidence. So I’d look for AI that can close that loop, rather than just generate more suggestions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI designing and running experiments but does not distinguish algorithmic discovery from synthetic data driving capability gains.

r002.rationale: It mentions testing more ideas in parallel, but does not identify additional compute as necessary for accelerating algorithmic progress.

r003.rationale: It describes AI taking on research tasks, but does not compare how quickly AI assistants and human collaborators can get up to speed.
